mean: to call black white on purpose, twisting the truth
lit: to point at a deer and call it a horse

story.text: Under the second emperor of Qin, the powerful official Zhao Gao wanted to find out who at court would dare oppose him. He presented a deer to the emperor and called it a horse. The emperor laughed and asked his ministers: some kept silent, some said 'horse' to please Zhao Gao, and some said 'deer'. Zhao Gao later had those who said 'deer' quietly punished.

use.how: Predicate, or 这是指鹿为马: deliberately calling something what it plainly is not, often by someone with power whom others dare not contradict.

near.diff: 颠倒黑白 is any reversal of right and wrong; 指鹿为马 stresses a knowing lie about plain facts, often by the powerful, testing who dares disagree.

cue: In a meeting, the boss calls an obvious flop a big success, and nobody in the room dares to say otherwise.

ctx.s: 明明是他迟到了，却说别人记错了时间，这不是{指鹿为马}吗？
ctx.en: He was the one who was late, yet he says everyone else got the time wrong. Isn't that calling a deer a horse?

ctx.s: 视频拍得清清楚楚，他还在{指鹿为马}，说那辆车没有闯红灯。
ctx.en: The video shows it perfectly clearly, and he still insists the car didn't run the red light.

ctx.s: 数据明摆着下降了，你在报告里写成增长，这就是{指鹿为马}。
ctx.en: The figures obviously went down, and you wrote them up as growth in the report. That's twisting the truth.

ctx.s: 老板把亏损说成“战略投入”，大家明知他在{指鹿为马}，却没人敢反驳。
ctx.en: The boss called the losses a 'strategic investment'; everyone knew he was twisting the facts, but no one dared object.

ctx.s: 在那个部门里，上司{指鹿为马}，下属也只好跟着点头。
ctx.en: In that department, when the boss calls a deer a horse, the staff can only nod along.

ctx.s: 历史上，有些权臣靠{指鹿为马}来试探谁敢跟自己作对。
ctx.en: In history, some powerful ministers used blatant lies to test who would dare stand against them.

bad.s: 他很会说话，经常{指鹿为马}，大家都喜欢听他讲故事。
bad.en: (meant: he is a vivid storyteller and everyone loves his stories)
bad.why: It condemns deliberately distorting facts; it is never praise for imaginative talk.

bad.s: 我把小王认成了小李，真是{指鹿为马}。
bad.en: (meant: I mistook Xiao Wang for Xiao Li)
bad.why: It is a knowing, deliberate lie, not an honest mistake of identification.

mean: to offer a humble, sincere apology
lit: to carry thorny sticks on one's back and ask to be punished

story.text: In the state of Zhao, Lin Xiangru was promoted above the veteran general Lian Po, who swore to humiliate him. Lin kept avoiding Lian Po, explaining that Qin did not dare attack Zhao only because the two of them stood together, and that a quarrel between them would help the enemy. Hearing this, Lian Po was ashamed. Bare-backed and carrying thorny sticks, he went to Lin's gate to beg forgiveness, and the two became close friends.

use.how: Intransitive predicate: 向某人负荆请罪, 上门负荆请罪. Going in person to admit a real fault; among friends often said half-jokingly.

near.diff: 赔礼道歉 is any ordinary apology; 负荆请罪 means humbling yourself, going in person and admitting you were seriously in the wrong.

cue: After insulting a teammate in a meeting, a man goes to her office the next morning, admits he was completely wrong, and asks her to forgive him.

ctx.s: 昨天是我不对，今天特地来向你{负荆请罪}。
ctx.en: I was in the wrong yesterday, so today I've come specially to apologise to you.

ctx.s: 他弄丢了朋友的相机，第二天带着一台新的上门{负荆请罪}。
ctx.en: He lost his friend's camera, and the next day he turned up at the door with a new one to apologise.

ctx.s: “说吧，你打算怎么{负荆请罪}？”妻子笑着问忘了纪念日的丈夫。
ctx.en: 'Well, how are you planning to make amends?' the wife asked, smiling, the husband who had forgotten their anniversary.

ctx.s: 两位老同事吵翻后，年长的那位主动{负荆请罪}，两人重归于好。
ctx.en: After the two old colleagues fell out, the older one went to apologise first, and they made up.

ctx.s: 产品出了严重的质量问题，总经理亲自到客户那里{负荆请罪}。
ctx.en: After a serious quality problem, the general manager went to the client in person to apologise.

ctx.s: 与其在背后找借口，不如痛快地{负荆请罪}，承认自己错了。
ctx.en: Rather than making excuses behind people's backs, you'd do better to apologise frankly and admit you were wrong.

bad.s: 我昨天{负荆请罪}他了。
bad.en: (meant: I apologised to him yesterday)
bad.why: It takes no object; the person you apologise to must come before it, introduced by 'to' (xiang).

bad.s: 法院判他{负荆请罪}三年。
bad.en: (meant: the court sentenced him to three years)
bad.why: It is a voluntary, humble apology, not a punishment that someone else imposes.

mean: to visit again and again to recruit talent
lit: to call three times at the thatched cottage

story.text: At the end of the Han dynasty, the warlord Liu Bei heard of Zhuge Liang, a brilliant young scholar living quietly in a thatched cottage. Liu Bei went in person to invite him; only on the third visit did he see him. Zhuge Liang agreed to serve him, and later wrote in his famous memorial that the late emperor had 'three times visited me in my thatched hut'.
story.source: 诸葛亮《出师表》；《三国志·蜀书·诸葛亮传》

use.how: Predicate, often 经过三顾茅庐 or …三顾茅庐才请来: someone in a higher position repeatedly and sincerely inviting a talented person to join.

near.diff: 礼贤下士 is a general habit of treating talented people with respect; 三顾茅庐 is repeated personal visits to win over one particular person.

cue: A start-up founder flies to another city three times to persuade a famous engineer to join her company, and only succeeds on the last visit.

ctx.s: 为了请这位老师来学校，校长{三顾茅庐}，终于打动了他。
ctx.en: To get this teacher to come to the school, the principal visited him again and again, and finally won him over.

ctx.s: 这位设计师是我们{三顾茅庐}才请来的，你可得好好配合她。
ctx.en: It took us repeated visits to get this designer to join, so make sure you work well with her.

ctx.s: 球队主帅{三顾茅庐}，才把这位退役名将请回来当助理教练。
ctx.en: Only after visiting him several times did the head coach persuade the retired star to come back as assistant coach.

ctx.s: 人家可是大专家，不{三顾茅庐}，怎么请得动？
ctx.en: He's a top expert. If you don't go and ask him in person again and again, how will you ever get him?

ctx.s: 他在回忆录里写道，正是对方的{三顾茅庐}让他下定了决心。
ctx.en: In his memoir he wrote that it was the other man's repeated visits that made up his mind.

ctx.s: 报社总编{三顾茅庐}，终于请这位老作家开了一个专栏。
ctx.en: The newspaper's chief editor called on the old writer time after time and finally got him to write a column.

bad.s: 我上个月{三顾茅庐}了奶奶家，陪她吃饭。
bad.en: (meant: last month I visited Grandma's several times to eat with her)
bad.why: It is about recruiting a talented person, not visiting family; it also takes no object.

bad.s: 他为了找到工作，向那家公司{三顾茅庐}。
bad.en: (meant: he kept applying to that company to get a job)
bad.why: The one who visits is the employer seeking talent, not a job seeker asking for work.

mean: panicked, seeing enemies on every side
lit: every blade of grass and every tree looks like a soldier

story.text: In 383, Fu Jian, ruler of the Former Qin, led a huge army south against the Eastern Jin. After an early setback he climbed the wall of Shouyang and saw the Jin troops drawn up in good order; looking at the grass and trees on Mount Bagong in the distance, he took them for soldiers too, and for the first time grew afraid. His army was soon routed at the Fei River.

use.how: Predicate, often after 弄得 or 吓得: describes people so tense that they take harmless things for threats. 大家草木皆兵。

near.diff: 惊弓之鸟 is a noun naming a person scarred by a past fright; 草木皆兵 describes the state of seeing danger everywhere.

cue: After a burglary on the street, residents think every rustle at night is a thief, and every stranger looks suspicious.

ctx.s: 别这么{草木皆兵}了，门外只是风吹树枝的声音。
ctx.en: Stop being so jumpy. That noise outside is just the wind in the branches.

ctx.s: 小区里刚丢了几辆电动车，大家{草木皆兵}，看谁都像小偷。
ctx.en: A few e-bikes were just stolen in the complex, and now everyone is on edge, seeing a thief in every face.

ctx.s: 流感一来，办公室里{草木皆兵}，谁咳嗽一声都有人躲开。
ctx.en: Once flu season hit, the office was in a panic: if anyone coughed, people moved away.

ctx.s: 公司传出裁员的消息，员工们{草木皆兵}，经理一皱眉就以为轮到自己了。
ctx.en: With rumours of layoffs, the staff are jittery; if the manager frowns they think they're next.

ctx.s: 股市大跌之后，投资者{草木皆兵}，一点小道消息就能引发抛售。
ctx.en: After the crash, investors are so nervous that the slightest rumour sets off a sell-off.

ctx.s: 那段时间他总觉得有人跟踪自己，弄得自己{草木皆兵}，晚上都不敢出门。
ctx.en: For a while he kept feeling he was being followed; he got so jumpy he didn't dare go out at night.

bad.s: 这个公园里{草木皆兵}，到处都是花草树木。
bad.en: (meant: the park is full of plants and trees everywhere)
bad.why: It is never about real vegetation; it describes panic that turns harmless things into imagined enemies.

bad.s: 我们的队伍{草木皆兵}，每个人都非常勇敢。
bad.en: (meant: our side is strong; everyone is brave)
bad.why: It describes fear and nervousness, not strength or courage.

mean: someone so scarred by a past fright they panic at any sign
lit: a bird frightened by the sound of a bow

story.text: The archer Geng Lei told the king of Wei that he could bring down a bird just by plucking his bowstring, with no arrow. A wild goose flew past; he twanged the string and it fell. He explained that the goose flew slowly and cried mournfully because an old wound had not healed and it had lost its flock. At the sound of the string it tried to climb in fright, the wound split open, and it dropped.

use.how: Noun phrase, usually 成了惊弓之鸟 or 像惊弓之鸟一样: a person who, after a bad experience, panics at the slightest hint of it again.

near.diff: 草木皆兵 describes a general state of seeing threats everywhere; 惊弓之鸟 names the person, and stresses the earlier shock behind the fear.

cue: Since being cheated by a phone scammer last year, an old man hangs up in terror whenever an unknown number calls.

ctx.s: 被狗咬过一次以后，他就成了{惊弓之鸟}，听到狗叫就躲。
ctx.en: Ever since he was bitten once, he's been terrified; he hides whenever he hears a dog bark.

ctx.s: 上次被骗了一大笔钱，她现在是{惊弓之鸟}，陌生电话一概不接。
ctx.en: After being cheated out of a lot of money, she's so scarred that she won't answer any unknown call.

ctx.s: 你别吓他了，他刚出过车祸，现在就像{惊弓之鸟}一样。
ctx.en: Don't scare him. He was just in a car accident and he's still jumping at everything.

ctx.s: 经历了那次大地震，很多居民成了{惊弓之鸟}，楼稍微一晃就往外跑。
ctx.en: After that big earthquake, many residents became so jumpy that they run outside at the slightest shake.

ctx.s: 被裁过一次的人，难免像{惊弓之鸟}，一听说公司重组就开始找下家。
ctx.en: People who've been laid off once tend to panic; at the first word of restructuring they start job-hunting.

ctx.s: 那伙劫匪已是{惊弓之鸟}，一听到警笛就四散逃跑。
ctx.en: The robbers were already badly rattled; at the first sound of a siren they scattered.

bad.s: 森林里有很多{惊弓之鸟}，叫声很好听。
bad.en: (meant: there are many birds in the forest with lovely songs)
bad.why: It is a figure for a frightened person, not a word for real birds.

bad.s: 他最近很{惊弓之鸟}。
bad.en: (meant: he has been very jumpy lately)
bad.why: It is a noun phrase and cannot be modified by 'very'; say he has 'become' a startled bird.

mean: to endure hardship while preparing a comeback
lit: to sleep on brushwood and taste bitter gall

story.text: Goujian, king of Yue, was defeated by the king of Wu and forced to submit. Back home, he kept a gall bladder by his seat and tasted its bitterness when sitting, lying down and eating, asking himself: have you forgotten the shame of Kuaiji? He lived plainly and rebuilt his state for many years, and finally destroyed Wu. The gall is in the Shiji; the brushwood bed was added in later retellings.

use.how: Predicate or modifier: 卧薪尝胆多年, 经过多年的卧薪尝胆. After a defeat or humiliation, enduring hardship for years to turn the tables.

near.diff: 破釜沉舟 is one decisive act that cuts off retreat; 卧薪尝胆 is years of quiet hardship after a defeat, waiting to rise again.

cue: After being humiliated in the final, a team spends four hard, quiet years rebuilding, and finally beats the same rival for the title.

ctx.s: 上次比赛惨败以后，他{卧薪尝胆}，苦练了整整三年。
ctx.en: After his crushing defeat last time, he gritted his teeth and trained hard for three whole years.

ctx.s: 落榜以后，他没有抱怨，而是{卧薪尝胆}，第二年考上了理想的大学。
ctx.en: After failing the exam he didn't complain; he buckled down through hard times and got into his dream university the next year.

ctx.s: 你现在需要的不是抱怨，而是{卧薪尝胆}，等待翻身的机会。
ctx.en: What you need now isn't complaining but quietly enduring and preparing until your chance to turn things around comes.

ctx.s: 公司被对手挤出市场后，创始人{卧薪尝胆}，十年后又重回行业前列。
ctx.en: Pushed out of the market by a rival, the founder endured and rebuilt, and ten years later was back among the industry leaders.

ctx.s: 经过多年的{卧薪尝胆}，这支球队终于在决赛中击败了老对手。
ctx.en: After years of hard, patient rebuilding, the team finally beat its old rival in the final.

ctx.s: 那段{卧薪尝胆}的日子虽然辛苦，却让她变得更加坚强。
ctx.en: Those years of enduring hardship to make a comeback were tough, but they made her stronger.

bad.s: 他学习很认真，每天都{卧薪尝胆}地背单词。
bad.en: (meant: he studies hard and memorises words every day)
bad.why: It needs an earlier defeat or humiliation and a long fight back; ordinary daily diligence does not call for it.

bad.s: 度假的时候，我们在海边{卧薪尝胆}，非常舒服。
bad.en: (meant: on holiday we relaxed by the sea, very comfortable)
bad.why: It means enduring deliberate hardship, the opposite of comfort and relaxation.

mean: to cut off all retreat, staking everything on success
lit: to smash the cooking pots and sink the boats

story.text: When a Qin army besieged Julu in the state of Zhao, Xiang Yu led his troops across the river to relieve it. Once across, he had all the boats sunk, the cooking pots smashed and the camp huts burned, and gave each soldier only three days' rations, to show there would be no going back. His men fought desperately and crushed the Qin army.

use.how: Predicate, or in 下定破釜沉舟的决心: making one decisive commitment and deliberately leaving no way back.

near.diff: 背水一战 is fighting a last-ditch battle with no way out; 破釜沉舟 stresses choosing to destroy your own way back beforehand.

cue: A man sells his flat and quits his secure job to put everything into his own restaurant, leaving himself nothing to fall back on.

ctx.s: 为了开这家店，她{破釜沉舟}，卖掉房子，断了自己的后路。
ctx.en: To open this shop she burned her bridges: she sold her flat and left herself no way back.

ctx.s: 他辞掉了稳定的工作，{破釜沉舟}，全力准备考研。
ctx.en: He quit his secure job and burned his bridges to prepare full-time for the graduate entrance exam.

ctx.s: “辞职信一交就收不回了，你真的要{破釜沉舟}吗？”朋友担心地问。
ctx.en: 'Once you hand in your resignation you can't take it back. Are you really going to burn your bridges?' his friend asked anxiously.

ctx.s: 他干脆{破釜沉舟}，把回国的机票退了，留在国外创业。
ctx.en: He simply burned his bridges: he cancelled his ticket home and stayed abroad to start his business.

ctx.s: 为了专心写完论文，她{破釜沉舟}，把所有游戏账号都注销了。
ctx.en: To focus on finishing her thesis, she cut off every escape route and deleted all her gaming accounts.

ctx.s: 下定了{破釜沉舟}的决心之后，他反而不再焦虑了。
ctx.en: Once he had resolved to leave himself no way back, he actually stopped feeling anxious.

bad.s: 我们{破釜沉舟}了很多年，终于把公司做大了。
bad.en: (meant: we struggled for many years and finally grew the company)
bad.why: It is a single decisive act of cutting off retreat, not years of steady effort.

bad.s: 他做饭时不小心{破釜沉舟}，把锅打碎了。
bad.en: (meant: while cooking he accidentally broke the pot)
bad.why: It is never about real pots or boats; it means a deliberate all-or-nothing decision.

lit: the Foolish Old Man moves the mountains

story.text: An old man of nearly ninety, called the Foolish Old Man, lived behind two great mountains, Taihang and Wangwu, which blocked his way. He set his family to digging them away and carrying the earth to the sea. A man called the Wise Old Man laughed at him. He replied that after him would come his sons and their sons without end, while the mountains would grow no higher. The mountain spirit, afraid he would never stop, told the Heavenly Emperor, who was moved by his sincerity and had the mountains carried away.

use.how: Mostly as a modifier: 愚公移山的精神, 愚公移山式的坚持. Praises patient effort, step by step, against a huge task.

near.diff: 卧薪尝胆 is enduring hardship after a defeat to get even; 愚公移山 is simply persisting at an enormous task, bit by bit, however long it takes.

cue: Villagers spend twenty years cutting a road through a cliff by hand, a little each year, though outsiders said it could never be done.

ctx.s: 老师给大家讲了{愚公移山}的故事，鼓励我们不要怕困难。
ctx.en: The teacher told us the story of the Foolish Old Man who moved the mountains, to encourage us not to fear difficulties.

ctx.s: 要背的单词这么多，只能像{愚公移山}一样，今天背一点，明天再背一点。
ctx.en: With so many words to learn, the only way is like the old man moving the mountains: a few today, a few more tomorrow.

ctx.s: 这些村民用了几十年修通山路，靠的就是{愚公移山}的精神。
ctx.en: These villagers took decades to build the mountain road, and what got them there was sheer perseverance.

ctx.s: 有人笑他们傻，可他们就像{愚公移山}一样，一年一年地在沙漠里种树。
ctx.en: Some laughed at them as fools, but like the old man moving the mountains they planted trees in the desert year after year.

ctx.s: 这么大的工程，难道真要{愚公移山}，一锹一锹地挖？
ctx.en: A project this big, are we really going to do it the Foolish Old Man's way, one shovelful at a time?

ctx.s: 治理这条河靠的不是一时的热情，而是{愚公移山}式的坚持。
ctx.en: Cleaning up this river takes not a burst of enthusiasm but mountain-moving persistence.

bad.s: 他太{愚公移山}了，一点也不聪明。
bad.en: (meant: he is too foolish, not clever at all)
bad.why: 'Foolish' is only the old man's nickname; the idiom praises perseverance and cannot be modified by 'too'.

bad.s: 我们公司明天{愚公移山}，搬到新办公楼去。
bad.en: (meant: our company moves to the new office building tomorrow)
bad.why: It is a figure for long, patient effort, not a word for moving house or office.

mean: to fail to make the list of those who passed an exam
lit: one's name falls below Sun Shan's

story.text: In the Song dynasty, a witty scholar named Sun Shan went to sit the prefectural examination together with the son of a man from his home town. Sun Shan passed, last on the list; the other young man failed. When the father asked how his son had done, Sun Shan answered with a line of verse: the last name on the list is Sun Shan, and your worthy son comes after Sun Shan.

use.how: Predicate, usually in narration: 他高考名落孙山. Failing an entrance exam or a selection; a gentler, bookish way to say someone did not get in.

near.diff: 一败涂地 is a crushing, total defeat; 名落孙山 only says someone did not make the list of those selected.

cue: The admissions list goes up, and a student reads it twice from top to bottom but cannot find his own name.

ctx.s: 他第一次考研{名落孙山}，第二年又考了一次。
ctx.en: He failed the graduate entrance exam the first time and sat it again the following year.

ctx.s: 去年公务员考试她{名落孙山}，今年准备得更充分了。
ctx.en: She didn't pass the civil service exam last year, so this year she has prepared more thoroughly.

ctx.s: “别灰心，一次{名落孙山}不代表什么。”妈妈安慰他。
ctx.en: 'Don't lose heart. Failing once doesn't mean anything,' his mother comforted him.

ctx.s: 这次选拔有一百多人参加，我不幸{名落孙山}。
ctx.en: Over a hundred people took part in the selection, and unfortunately I didn't make the cut.

ctx.s: 听说表哥{名落孙山}，全家都没敢在饭桌上提考试的事。
ctx.en: Hearing that my cousin had failed, no one in the family dared mention exams at the dinner table.

ctx.s: 当年{名落孙山}的少年，后来成了有名的作家。
ctx.en: The boy who once failed the exam later became a famous writer.

bad.s: 他在比赛中{名落孙山}，得了第一名。
bad.en: (meant: he made a name for himself and won first place)
bad.why: It means failing to be selected, the opposite of winning.

bad.s: 这位歌手早已{名落孙山}，大家都不记得他了。
bad.en: (meant: the singer has long faded from fame)
bad.why: It is about failing an exam or selection, not about losing one's fame.

mean: to volunteer oneself for a task

story.text: When Qin besieged the Zhao capital, Lord Pingyuan was sent to Chu to seek an alliance and wanted twenty able retainers to go with him, but found only nineteen. Mao Sui, a retainer who had done nothing notable in three years, put himself forward. The lord said a talented man is like an awl in a bag, whose point soon shows; Mao Sui replied that he was asking to be put in the bag today. In Chu, when talks stalled, Mao Sui stepped up, sword in hand, and argued until the king of Chu agreed.

use.how: Intransitive predicate, often 我毛遂自荐一下 or 他毛遂自荐当…: putting oneself forward as the right person for a role or job.

near.diff: 自告奋勇 is eagerly volunteering for a hard or risky task; 毛遂自荐 is recommending yourself as qualified for a post or role.

cue: A company is looking for someone to lead a new project, and a junior employee nobody had noticed writes to the boss explaining why she is the right person for it.

ctx.s: 我{毛遂自荐}一下，我学过设计，海报可以交给我来做。
ctx.en: Let me put myself forward: I've studied design, so you can leave the poster to me.

ctx.s: “有谁愿意负责这次活动？”“我想{毛遂自荐}。”
ctx.en: 'Who would like to be in charge of this event?' 'I'd like to put my own name forward.'

ctx.s: 班里要选一个主持人，小林{毛遂自荐}，说自己以前主持过晚会。
ctx.en: The class needed a host, and Xiao Lin put himself forward, saying he had hosted parties before.

ctx.s: 公司招人的时候，他主动写信{毛遂自荐}，结果真的被录用了。
ctx.en: When the company was hiring, he wrote in on his own initiative recommending himself, and he actually got the job.

ctx.s: 没想到这次是她{毛遂自荐}，当上了项目负责人。
ctx.en: No one expected that she would put herself forward this time and end up as project lead.

ctx.s: 与其等着别人发现你，不如大胆地{毛遂自荐}。
ctx.en: Rather than waiting for others to discover you, you'd do better to boldly put yourself forward.

bad.s: 我{毛遂自荐}他当班长，因为他很负责。
bad.en: (meant: I recommend him as class monitor because he is responsible)
bad.why: The second half means recommending yourself; it cannot take another person as its object.

bad.s: 他喜欢{毛遂自荐}，到处说自己多么了不起。
bad.en: (meant: he loves to brag about how great he is)
bad.why: It is offering yourself for a specific role, not general boasting about yourself.
